wachiman.text:
canManage() grants manage to admins that only have the VIEW scope

`canManage()` calls `hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE)`, so an admin with only an all-groups `view` permission passes. `GroupsResource` line 181 uses `auth.groups().requireManage()` to guard creating top-level groups, so a view-only admin can create them. The sibling `ClientPermissionsV2.canManage()` (line 73) checks `MANAGE` only, and so does the per-group `canManage(GroupModel)` at line 79. Use `hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)`. The new Javadoc on `GroupPermissionEvaluator.canManage()` (lines 75-76) documents the same mistake and should be corrected too. `testViewGroups` does not catch this because it never tries a write with a view-only permission.

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission iterates the wrong resources and returns resource UUIDs instead of group IDs

Per-group resources are created in `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource` (lines 118-127) with the group id as `name` and no `setType`. Only the all-groups resource (named "Groups") gets type `Groups`, in `init` at line 274. So `findByType(server, GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...)` appears to return only the all-groups type resource. On top of that, the lambda passes `groupResource.getId()`, which is the resource UUID, to `hasPermission`. That method looks it up with `findByName(server, groupId)`, where the name is the group id, so it falls back to the all-groups resource. Finally it adds `groupResource.getId()` (a resource UUID, not a group id) to the result. Consequences:
- An admin with only per-group `view-members` gets an empty set. `searchForUser` then sets no `UserModel.GROUPS` restriction, so the DB query is unrestricted and relies on the post-filter. Counts from `getUsersCount(..., groupIds)` are wrong, and paging is applied before the filter.
- An admin with all-groups `view-members` gets a set containing a non-group UUID. That set is applied as the group restriction in `JpaUserProvider` (around line 762), so the search returns no users.

The tests pass only because the post-filter `canView(user)` goes through `canViewMembers`. Iterate resources by name, or iterate the realm's groups, use the group id for both the lookup and the result, and add a test for the user count and for all-groups `view-members`.

Realms that already enabled admin permissions have no Groups type resource or new scopes

`AdminPermissionsSchema.init` returns early when the permissions client already exists (line 250). A realm that enabled V2 before this change therefore has no `Groups` resource and none of the `manage-membership`, `manage-members` or `view-members` scopes. In that case `getResourceTypeResource` returns null, and `policyStore.findByResource(server, null)` here (and `resource.getScopes()` at line 152) would likely throw. `canViewByGroup`, `canView(group)` and similar calls would then fail for every non-role admin in that realm. `getOrCreateResource` would also throw "No scopes found." Is there a migration or lazy init for existing V2 realms, or is that accepted because the feature is experimental?

Group removal listener now hits a V2 groups() that throws UnsupportedOperationException when both FGAP flags are on

The listener is registered when `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ` (V1) is enabled, but `management()` returns `MgmtPermissionsV2` whenever `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2` is enabled. The V2 flag does not depend on V1 (Profile.java line 58). With both flags on, deleting a group now reaches `GroupPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled`, which throws. Before this change `groups()` was always the V1 class, so the delete worked. Client removal already has the same problem via `ClientPermissionsV2`. The tests enable only V2, so they do not exercise this. Make the listener skip V2, or have the V2 methods do nothing when called from it.

Javadoc inaccuracies

`requireManageMembers` (line 133) says it throws when `canManageMembership` is false; it should reference `canManageMembers`. `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission` (line 145) says it returns a "Stream" but returns `Set<String>`. The `canManage()` doc (lines 75-76) says VIEW grants manage, which is the bug reported on `GroupPermissionsV2.java` line 70.

Missing negative and count coverage

`testViewGroups` never checks that a view-only admin cannot create or modify groups, which would have caught the `canManage()` bug. No test covers an all-groups `view-members` or `manage-members` permission, or `users().count()` for an admin with group-scoped permissions. Those are the paths that use `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission`. Line 68 also has a stray `;;`.

Fail-fast on multiple crypto providers removed; equal-order providers are now picked silently

Before this change, more than one CryptoProvider on the classpath threw `IllegalStateException`. Now the providers are sorted by `order()` and the first one wins. The default, elytron and fips1402 providers all return 200 (`DefaultCryptoProvider.java:84`, `WildFlyElytronProvider.java:77`, `FIPS1402Provider.java:115`). If two of them are on the classpath, the winner depends on `ServiceLoader` iteration order, which follows classpath order and is stable in the sort. A FIPS deployment that also has the default provider on the classpath could then silently run non-FIPS crypto. The only trace is a `debug` log. The misconfiguration error is the only safeguard that was removed, and only the intended authz-client case (100 vs 200) needs the new behaviour. Suggested fix: throw the previous error when the top two providers have the same `order()`. At minimum, log the ignored providers at WARN.

New abstract `order()` breaks every external CryptoProvider implementation

`CryptoProvider` is a public SPI interface in `common`. Adding an abstract `int order()` stops any out-of-tree implementation from compiling. A custom provider that was already compiled will fail with `AbstractMethodError` inside the sort in `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider`. A `default int order() { return 200; }` (or similar) would keep source and binary compatibility and still allow the authz-client provider to override it.

Dead statements in concatenatedRSToASN1DER

Lines 114-115 build two `ASN1Encoder` instances and discard them. The result is rebuilt on lines 117-121. Remove them.

Malformed DER yields unchecked exceptions instead of IOException

`readInteger` on `02 80` gets length -1 from `readLength` (indefinite form), and `read(-1)` throws `NegativeArraySizeException`. A zero-length INTEGER makes `new BigInteger(new byte[0])` throw `NumberFormatException`. `readNext` also mishandles a nested indefinite length (`length += reset()` with length -1). The `ECDSACryptoProvider` contract and the callers declare `IOException`, and the current callers happen to catch `Exception`. The only caller today feeds this decoder trusted JDK-produced DER, so impact is low. Reject negative lengths in `readLength` and `readInteger`, and reject empty integers, so the decoder fails with `IOException`. Also, `readTagNumber` masks the class and constructed bits, so a primitive tag 0x10 passes as a SEQUENCE. Compare the full tag byte.

Test uses a P-256 key for ES384/ES512 and only checks self round-trip

`KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()` gives a 256-bit curve key. For ES384 and ES512 the signature is therefore r and s of at most 32 bytes padded into 48- and 66-byte halves. The real P-384 and P-521 value sizes are never exercised. The key and signature are random, so the cases that matter (high-bit r or s, short r or s that needs padding or a stripped leading zero) are hit only by chance and the test can pass or fail from run to run. The assertion compares the provider's output with its own re-encoding. It never checks that the re-encoded DER verifies with `Signature.verify`, and it never compares against the BC implementation. Suggested: generate a key per curve (`secp256r1`, `secp384r1`, `secp521r1`), verify the re-encoded DER with `Signature.verify`, and add fixed vectors with short and high-bit r and s. `hamcrest` is added to the pom (`authz/client/pom.xml:67-71`) but is not used by the test.

First-wins CryptoIntegration.init in a library entry point

`CryptoIntegration.init` does nothing once a provider has been set, and it uses the classloader passed by the first caller. If an application calls `AuthzClient.create` before the intended full provider is initialised (for example, crypto jars loaded by a different classloader than the authz-client jar), only the 100-order provider sees `AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()`. It is then latched for the whole JVM, and every unsupported operation (`getCertificateUtils`, `getSignature`, ...) throws `UnsupportedOperationException`. Is this ordering scenario considered, and is it documented?

Reader thread is never joined, so the assertion can run before the reader finishes and the test can pass without detecting the bug

The reader thread is started with `new Thread(...).start()` and never joined. After the last delete, `deletedAll.set(true)` is followed at once by `assertThat(caughtExceptions, empty())`. A request that is still in flight in the reader can throw after the assertion has run, and the test passes. The thread is also not a daemon thread. If an assertion or delete fails earlier, `deletedAll` is never set and the reader loops forever, which can hang the JVM. Keep the Thread reference. Set the flag in a `finally` block, call `join()` with a timeout, and only then assert. An ExecutorService or CompletableFuture would also work. Also consider asserting that the reader completed at least one iteration while deletes were running, so the test shows it exercised the concurrency.

Reader only exercises the brief listing with subGroupCount

`groups(null, 0, Integer.MAX_VALUE, true)` appears to be the path that reaches `GroupUtils.populateSubGroupCount` and `GroupAdapter.getSubGroupsCount`. That is the only path this PR fixes. Other `GroupAdapter` methods that dereference `modelSupplier.get()` unguarded (the `getSubGroupsStream(...)` overloads at GroupAdapter.java:256, 262 and 268) are not covered. The same applies to `session.groups().getGroupById` returning null for `parentModel` in GroupUtils.java:47-57. Whether the test fails without the fix depends on timing, so it can be flaky as a regression test.

Fix covers only getSubGroupsCount; sibling methods still NPE on a concurrently deleted group

`getSubGroupsStream(search, first, max)`, `getSubGroupsStream(first, max)` and `getSubGroupsStream(search, exact, first, max)` (lines 256, 262, 268) still call `modelSupplier.get().…` with no null check. `LazyModel` wraps `getGroupModel()`, which can return null once the group is deleted. These methods have the same failure mode as the one fixed here. `populateGroupHierarchyFromSubGroups` in GroupUtils.java:47-57 also uses `parentModel` without a null check. Returning null from `getSubGroupsCount()` is tolerated by `GroupRepresentation.setSubGroupCount(Long)`, so that change is safe. Decide whether the other methods should be guarded the same way, or whether a deleted group should be filtered out earlier.

Style nits in the new test

Line 117 is a whitespace-only line. The test name `createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti` does not say what is verified. The variable `groupUuuids` is misspelled. The test imports `org.hamcrest.Matchers` while the file already static-imports other matchers, so `empty` could be statically imported to match the file's convention.

Call to isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() with no arguments does not compile

The only definition of `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled` in the repository is `UsernamePasswordForm.isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` (UsernamePasswordForm.java:160). A grep over all *.java files finds no no-arg overload. `UsernameForm.authenticate` calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()`, so the `services` module fails to compile and nothing in this PR can build or run. Pass the user instead: `if (context.getUser() != null && !isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser()))`.

`user != null` condition disables passkeys on the initial (unidentified) login

Before this change, the passkey setup in `authenticate` ran only when the user was NOT yet identified, and `challenge(...)` on error ran only when `context.getUser() == null`. The new helper returns `webauthnAuth != null && isPasskeysEnabled() && user != null`, so `fillContextForm` is now called only when a user is already set. In a normal first login `context.getUser()` is null: `authenticate` takes the `else` branch (line 103) and `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(null)` at line 115 is false. The login page is then rendered without the conditional-UI attributes (challenge, rpId, `ENABLE_WEBAUTHN_CONDITIONAL_UI`). The same applies to the error path at line 137, because `getUser` clears the user before a failed username/password check. This breaks the main passkeys feature. The existing tests assert it, for example `PasskeysUsernamePasswordFormTest.webauthnLoginWithDiscoverableKey` (auto-login) and `passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey` (`//form[@id='webauth']` present and autocomplete `username webauthn` on the first page). It also looks inverted against the intended behaviour: the Organization test expects the webauthn form with the user already selected. The condition should allow `user == null`. For a set user it should probably check that the user has a passwordless credential (`user.credentialManager().isConfiguredFor(webauthnAuth.getCredentialType())`). That would also make the `reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey` comment true.

reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey does not cover a user without passkey

The comment says passkeys should not be shown during re-authentication because "this user does not have passkey". The test actually disables passkeys at realm level (`setWebAuthnPolicyPasskeysEnabled(FALSE)`), so it only checks the realm switch. The case of a realm with passkeys enabled and a re-authenticating user who has no passkey is untested. The current helper (`user != null`) would show the passkey form to such a user. Add a test with passkeys enabled and a password-only user, or fix the comment. Separately, `catch (Exception nsee)` around `findElement`/`fail` is a weak pattern. `Assert.assertThrows(NoSuchElementException.class, ...)`, as used in the Organization test, is clearer.

webauthnLoginWithExternalKey_reauthentication largely duplicates other tests

The first half is a verbatim copy of `passwordLoginWithExternalKey` (lines 172-210), and the re-authentication half is covered again by `webauthnLoginWithExternalKey_reauthenticationWithPasswordOrPasskey`. The shared setup could be pulled into a helper like `setPasswordlessPolicyForExternalKey`. The duplicated test also lengthens the already-slow browser suite.

Missing @Override on overriding method

`shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators` overrides the protected method added in `WebAuthnAuthenticator`, but has no `@Override`. Add it so a later signature change in the parent is caught at compile time.

Hung flusher is no longer killed on restart (isinstance check never matches SpawnProcess)

The old code called `self.process.kill()` unconditionally. The new code only kills `if isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`. The processes are created with `self.mp_context.Process` (line 105) from a `spawn` context. As far as I know, `SpawnProcess` subclasses `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess`, not `multiprocessing.context.Process` (which is what `multiprocessing.Process` is). If so, the check is always False for real processes. I did not run it.

Then the `cause == "hang"` branch (line 236) starts a replacement via `_create_process_for_shards` (line 259) without stopping the hung one. Two flushers now run over the same shards, and the old one is dropped from `self.processes`. Both can flush the same segments, producing duplicates to buffered-segments. Each restart cycle leaks another process, up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS.

The same check in `join` (line 346) means `terminate()` is also skipped. That is not new, but the guard is new at line 254. Check against `threading.Thread` instead, or just call `kill()` when the object has it. CLAUDE.md's new hasattr-to-isinstance guidance does not apply to this case, because here the isinstance target is the wrong type.

join() skips terminating remaining processes once the deadline passes

When `remaining_time <= 0` the loop `break`s, so every later process skips the `terminate()` call at line 347. The old code always terminated after waiting. Terminate each process regardless of the deadline, and only skip the waiting part.

Memory info is queried once per sub-buffer against the same Redis

`SpansBuffer.get_memory_info` returns `iter_cluster_memory_usage(self.client)` (buffer.py:375-376), which covers the whole cluster, not the buffer's shards. Each sub-buffer is built from the same config, so the loop at lines 300-301 repeats the same cluster scan N times per `submit` when `max-memory-percentage < 1.0`. It also duplicates every entry in `memory_infos`. The ratio comes out the same, but the work scales with flusher_processes. Query one buffer instead. The same applies to `record_stored_segments` at lines 269-270, which issues N pipelines for shards that one call could cover.

Inconsistent metric tag names and high-cardinality tag value

`spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `segment_size_bytes` use the tag `shard`, while `wait_produce` (line 199) uses `shards`. `flusher_unhealthy` uses `shard` with a single shard id (line 244). The `shard_tag` value is the comma-joined list of all shards the process owns. With the default of one process, that is every assigned partition in one tag value. It changes with every rebalance, which hurts cardinality and makes dashboards hard to build. Pick one tag name, and consider tagging by process index.

Docstring says one process per shard, but the count is capped by max_processes

The class docstring says "Creates one process per shard". The code creates `min(max_processes, len(assigned_shards))` processes. The CLI default of 1 (consumers/__init__.py:434) gives a single process for all shards, and a larger value shares shards between processes.

time.sleep(0.1) in the test is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched

Line 15 does `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`, which patches the `time` module attribute globally. The test's own `time.sleep(0.1)` at line 62 therefore does nothing, so the "give flusher threads time" step does not wait. The test still relies on the race between the flusher threads and `step.join()` setting `stopped`. Poll for `messages` with a real deadline, using `time.monotonic` and a short loop. Capture the real sleep before patching if a sleep is needed.

test_flusher_processes_limit only checks bookkeeping, and leaves the flusher threads spinning

The test asserts the shard-to-process map but never feeds a span, so it does not check that segments from every shard are flushed or that restart works. `messages` and `commits` are unused. `time.sleep` is patched to a no-op, so the flusher threads busy-loop against Redis until `join`. There is also no test for `flusher_processes=None` (one process per shard), for the hang or crash restart path, or for the CLI option reaching the factory.

Backpressure assertion is weaker than before

`any(x.value for ...)` passes if any single process is backpressured. That is fine for the single-process setup here. Nothing covers `submit` rejecting when only one of several processes is backpressured, which is the new behaviour at flusher.py:278-284.

Flex.Item grow={1} is not equivalent to the removed `flex: 1`

The removed `FlexContainer` used `flex: 1`, which is `1 1 0%`. `<Flex.Item grow={1}>` renders `flex-grow:1; flex-shrink:1; flex-basis:auto` (static/app/components/core/layout/flex.tsx:35-46). With basis `auto`, the description and feature list start at their content width. The sibling `Metadata` block (line 265; it sets no flex properties and so shrinks by default) is then squeezed when the description is long. Before, the description started at 0 and only took the leftover space. `Flex.Item` accepts `flex`, so `<Flex.Item flex="1">` keeps the old layout.

New title truncation and environment lookup are not covered

The comment format now goes through `get_merged_pr_single_issue_template`, `_truncate_title` (50 characters) and `get_environment_info` (src/sentry/integrations/source_code_management/commit_context.py:577-606). The tests only use short titles and one dev/prod environment. Nothing covers a title over 50 characters, or the `except Exception` fallback in `get_environment_info` that returns an empty string. The GitLab tests have the same gap, because both integrations share this code. A test with a long title and one where `get_recommended_event` raises would pin the behaviour.

Age/timestamp exclusivity tests miss the falsy and neither-present cases

The serializer checks exclusivity with truthiness (`self.initial_data.get("age")` and `.get("timestamp")` in src/sentry/issues/endpoints/browser_reporting_collector.py:52 and :58). `test_mixed_fields` only sends `age=1` with a nonzero timestamp. A report with `age=0` and a `timestamp`, which the validators accept, is untested. So is a report with neither field, which `required=False` also accepts. Add cases that assert the intended behaviour, or tighten the validators to check `is not None` and add a test for that.

max_segment_id=None here is never exercised

`delete_matched_rows` is patched in this test (line 82), so the `None` row is only passed to a mock. The null handling lives in `_make_recording_filenames` (src/sentry/replays/usecases/delete.py:89). Changing the fixture value does not test it. Add or point to a test of `_make_recording_filenames`/`delete_matched_rows` with `max_segment_id=None`. Note also that `run_bulk_replay_delete_job` and the `delete_replays_script_async` paths in src/sentry/replays/tasks.py (lines 91 and 251) still type `max_segment_id: int`.

New 'Project not found' branch has no test

The project now comes from `replayRecord.project_id`, and a new error state renders when that project is not in the projects store. There is no spec in `static/app/views/replays/detail/ai/`. A test for this branch would also cover the switch away from the `project` query param.

Tests use seconds for both breadcrumb and error timestamps, which hides a likely unit mismatch in the merge order

`gen_request_data` (src/sentry/replays/endpoints/project_replay_summarize_breadcrumbs.py:153-155) compares each error's `timestamp` with each recording event's top-level `timestamp`. The error timestamp comes from nodestore and is in epoch seconds. Replay recording events are rrweb events, and I believe their `timestamp` is in epoch milliseconds. `event_parser.py:387` treats a payload timestamp as an int, but I did not find a conversion to seconds. If the units differ, every error timestamp (~1.7e9) is smaller than every event timestamp (~1.7e12). All errors would then be emitted before all breadcrumbs, and the summary would get a wrong timeline with no error. The new tests cannot catch this. `test_get_with_error` uses `now.timestamp()` for the segment event (line 254 in the sibling test, line 188 in the first) and `now.timestamp() - 1` for the error. `test_get_request_data` uses 1.0–3.0 for both. Use a realistic millisecond timestamp for the recording events, and assert the position of the error line relative to the breadcrumb line. Confirm the unit in the producer or the frontend, then fix the comparison in the endpoint if they differ.

The `division by zero` assertion does not show that `message` is populated

`fetch_error_details` fills `title` from `data['title']` and `message` from `data['message']`. For an event stored with an `exception`, the title is probably `ZeroDivisionError: division by zero`. The line is built as `'{title}: {message}'`, so both substring asserts pass from the title alone. They would pass even if `message` were empty. If `message` matters, assert on the full formatted line. Otherwise drop the second assert so it does not suggest coverage it lacks.

`member.has_global_access` is evaluated on every request and `member` can be None

`RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is typed `RpcOrganizationMember | None` (src/sentry/organizations/services/organization/model.py:346). `enable_advanced` is computed unconditionally, before `use_optimized` is checked. For a non-superuser request with no member (for example some token or API-key callers), `organization_context.member.has_global_access` raises AttributeError. That breaks the plain default listing, which worked before. Short-circuit on `use_optimized` first, and guard `member is None`. Also use `is_active_superuser(request)` rather than `request.user.is_superuser`, which is true for a superuser who has not activated a superuser session.

OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot paginate the datetime key; `optimized_pagination=true` fails whenever there are rows

The endpoint passes `order_by="-datetime"`. The new class copies `Paginator.get_item_key` and `value_from_cursor` (integer key), not the `DateTimePaginator` versions. `math.floor(getattr(item, "datetime"))` on a `datetime` raises TypeError, so any non-empty page is a 500 (`build_cursor` calls `key` on the results). `value_from_cursor` returns the raw number, where `build_queryset` needs a datetime for the `datetime >=/<= %s` comparison. A follow-up cursor would therefore compare a timestamp×1000 number against a datetime column. The new path is not usable for audit logs. The PR adds no tests, so nothing caught this. Subclass `DateTimePaginator` or reuse its key and cursor-value logic.

Negative-offset branch is unsupported by Django and its comments are false; a user-supplied negative cursor offset is accepted

`Cursor.from_string` accepts a negative offset (`int(bits[1])`, src/sentry/utils/cursors.py:59), so a client can send `cursor=0:-N:1`. Django querysets do not support negative slicing: `queryset[-5:x]` raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported`. The comments at 874-880 ("Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically", "access to data beyond normal pagination bounds", "safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level") are wrong. The feature is unreachable in a working form, and its only effect is a 500 on crafted input. Even if slicing worked, `stop = start + limit + extra` with a negative start would return a truncated, wrong page. Remove the negative-offset path and the `enable_advanced_features` flag. If the aim is faster reverse pagination, implement it with real queryset ordering.

Shared BasePaginator now silently clamps negative offsets, and the comment contradicts the code

This hunk changes `BasePaginator.get_result`, which every `Paginator`/`DateTimePaginator` subclass uses. Previously a negative offset was never normalised. Now, when `not cursor.is_prev`, it is clamped to 0, so a malformed cursor returns page 1 data instead of failing. For `is_prev` it still passes the negative offset through unchanged. The comment says negative offsets are being allowed "to enable efficient bidirectional pagination" and that the queryset "will handle boundary conditions". The code does the opposite for forward cursors, and Django does not handle negative slices. The line 192 check `len(results) == offset + limit + extra` still uses the unclamped `offset`, so it disagrees with `start_offset`. It is unrelated to the stated goal and changes behavior for all callers with no tests. Revert it.

OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates BasePaginator.get_result and adds no optimization

Lines 845-911 copy `BasePaginator.get_result` almost line for line. The only difference is the negative-offset branch, which cannot work (see the other finding). Nothing in the class is optimized, so the docstring claims ("optimized query path", "streamlined boundary condition handling") are untrue. The else branch repeats the base logic. The `offset + limit + extra` check at line 891 uses the unclamped offset. Drop the class, or if a real optimization is intended, express only the difference. Also, at lines 819-820 there are two extra blank lines, and the endpoint has trailing whitespace on lines 72 and 89.

What does the `optimized_pagination` switch do for audit-log users, and why is it gated by role?

The audit log endpoint is permission-gated by `OrganizationAuditPermission`. A query-param switch that selects a different paginator for superusers/global-access members is an undocumented API surface that the PR body ("Enhanced Pagination Performance") does not explain. The only behavioral difference is the negative-offset path, so the gating suggests it exposes something beyond normal bounds. The audit-log data is already restricted to `organization_id`, so the gating buys nothing. Please state the intended user-visible benefit, or remove the flag.

TotalDocs ranges over b.cache without cacheMu; BuildIndex now writes it concurrently

`TotalDocs` iterates `b.cache` with no lock. This PR adds a call to it at `pkg/storage/unified/resource/search.go:216`, after the goroutine that runs `handleEvent` has started (search.go:207-213). `handleEvent` calls `getOrCreateIndex`, which calls `BuildIndex`, and that writes `b.cache[key]` at bleve.go:138 under `cacheMu`. `TotalDocs` takes no lock, so an event arriving during init, or a Prometheus scrape through `bleve_index_metrics.go:96`, can read the map while it is being written. Go aborts the process on a concurrent map read and write. The PR also removes the function-wide lock from `BuildIndex`, so a write to the map can now happen at any time while the metrics collector reads it. Take `b.cacheMu.RLock()` in `TotalDocs`. Note that `DocCount` on each index is called under the lock, which is fine.

Index build and lifecycle Init now run synchronously inside NewResourceServer, and lifecycle Init gets the server's own context

`Init` now runs in the constructor: `lifecycle.Init`, a full `search.init` (which indexes every resource above the minimum count) and `initWatcher`. Any error makes construction fail, so a search-index failure now stops the whole apiserver or module from starting. Before, the first request returned the error and the server still constructed. Construction time also now grows with data size. `Init` is also called with the background context that carries the admin `watcher` identity (server.go:229-235), not a request context, which is probably intended but changes what the backend sees. Separately, the per-RPC `Init` checks are removed, so after `Stop` sets `initErr` (server.go:321-339), requests no longer return 'service is stopping'. Please confirm that fail-fast startup and the loss of the post-Stop rejection are intended. The PR body ('Unified Storage Performance Optimizations') says neither.

Postgres integration test skipped without explanation in the PR

The test is skipped for postgres with 'not working ... in Drone'. The PR also moves resource-server initialization into the constructor, which could change startup behaviour for this storage-server target. Please confirm the failure is not caused by this change. Strategy close() shuts down the factory-owned queue pool; the next strategy after a rebalance silently drops messages

The `FixedQueuePool` is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` (result_consumer.py:131-137) and handed to every strategy that `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker` builds (result_consumer.py:254-255). `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()`/`terminate()`/`join()` call `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` (queue_consumer.py:335-345). Arroyo closes the strategy on every partition revocation and then calls `create_with_partitions` again on the same factory. That call reuses `self.queue_pool`, whose queues are shut down and whose workers have exited.

In the new strategy, `FixedQueuePool.submit` calls `offset_tracker.add_offset` (line 211) and then `work_queue.put` (line 212), which raises `queue.ShutDown`. The `except Exception` in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` (lines 317-325) logs it and then calls `add_offset` and `complete_offset` for that offset. Every message after the first rebalance is therefore marked complete without being processed, and the commit loop commits those offsets. The same shared state causes a second problem. `OffsetTracker` persists across strategies, so offsets that were queued but never run when the workers exited (the `shutdown` flag stops the loop with items still queued) stay in `outstanding` forever. If the partition is reassigned to this consumer, it can never commit past them.

Fix: have each strategy own its pool and tracker, or create the pool lazily in `create_with_partitions`. Alternatively, make `close()` stop only the strategy's commit thread and leave pool shutdown to `factory.shutdown()`. If the pool is kept, reset the tracker on assign. Add a test that creates, closes and re-creates a strategy from the same factory, then submits a message.

If processing (DB and Redis work in `handle_result`) is slower than the topic rate, or one hot group sits behind a slow worker, the consumer keeps polling Kafka and holds every message in memory. `OffsetTracker.all_offsets` also grows without bound, and a stalled commit makes that worse. Other modes get bounded memory from the batch size limits or `MessageRejected`.

Submit-error path marks the offset complete, which contradicts the "no item is lost" guarantee

`commit_function` is called from a background thread, not the consumer thread

`_commit_loop` runs in its own thread and calls the arroyo `commit` callable (wrapped in `commit_offsets`, result_consumer.py:249-252). Arroyo's `StreamProcessor` commit stages offsets on the Kafka consumer. That consumer is driven from the main thread (`poll`, `pause`, `resume`). Every other mode in this factory commits from the main thread via `CommitOffsets` in `poll`/`submit`. The consumer's staged-offset state is not documented as thread-safe, so a race with `poll` or rebalance callbacks is possible. After a revoke, committing for a partition that is no longer assigned also raises. Because `mark_committed` is skipped on exception, the loop retries and logs `Error in commit loop` every second until the partition is reassigned. A safer design is for the worker threads to record completions and for `poll()`, on the consumer thread, to compute and call `commit`. If the background thread is kept, say why it is safe.

Any gap in Kafka offsets stalls commits for the partition permanently

`get_committable_offsets` breaks at the first offset in `range(start, max_offset+1)` that is not in `all_offsets`. Kafka offsets are not guaranteed to be contiguous: transaction markers, compaction and similar events leave gaps. A missing offset is never in `all_offsets`, so the partition never commits past it, and the `all_offsets` set grows without bound. `test_offset_gaps_block_commits` asserts exactly this behaviour. It is correct for a delayed message but wrong for a real gap, and it cannot tell the two apart. Consider tracking by arrival order instead: treat the lowest outstanding offset as the commit boundary, so the committable offset is `min(outstanding) - 1`, or the highest seen offset if nothing is outstanding. That also removes the O(range) loop under the lock.

Shutdown wait is per-worker, so the worst case is about 5s × num_queues + 5s

`FixedQueuePool.shutdown` joins each worker with `timeout=5.0` in sequence (lines 242-243), and `close()` first spends up to 5s on the commit thread (line 337). With the default 20 workers, if every worker is stuck in a slow `handle_result`, the revoke or shutdown callback blocks for about 105s. Arroyo runs `close`/`join` inside the rebalance callback. That is enough to exceed `max.poll.interval.ms` or the session timeout and get the consumer kicked from the group. Use one overall deadline (`deadline = time.monotonic() + 5`, then `join(max(0, deadline - now))`). Note also that `shutdown=True` makes workers exit with items still queued, so the `immediate=False` drain never actually drains.

Async legacy writes inherit the request context and swallow their errors

The legacy write in Create (50-57), Delete (108-114), Update (134-141) and DeleteCollection (161-167) runs in a goroutine. Its context is derived from the request `ctx` through `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`. The handler returns right after launching the goroutine. In the k8s apiserver the request context is cancelled when the handler returns, so the legacy write can be cancelled before it runs or while it is running. The legacy store can then silently miss writes. The new 10s timeout does not help, because the parent's cancellation wins. Use a context detached from the request's cancellation, for example `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` wrapped in the timeout, so the logger and values are kept. The goroutines also never log a legacy error. They only record a metric, so a failed legacy write leaves no log line. The old code logged `unable to create object in legacy storage`. Add `log.Error` in each goroutine. I did not read the apiserver handler code that cancels the request context, so confidence is medium.

`Post#cook` now returns `raw` untouched for `cook_method == raw_html`. The only producers are `TopicEmbed.import` callers, and their input is third-party HTML. `PollFeed` passes `CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` (poll_feed.rb:35), so a feed item containing `<script>` or `onerror=` is unescaped into live markup. `import_remote` passes Readability output, whose whitelist (topic_embed.rb:48-50) keeps `href`, so `javascript:` links survive. `absolutize_urls` only rewrites URLs and calls `to_html` (topic_embed.rb:75). Relative values without a leading slash (`images/a.png`, `../x`) are not absolutized at all. The action lowers the level one step each time it runs: above regular goes to regular, otherwise to muted. The route is a GET that renders a full page. A watching or tracking user who clicks once becomes regular, and a second hit makes them muted. The page text is the same both times (`topic.unsubscribe.stop_notifications`). A confirm step that the user submits as a POST also fixes it.

I did not check whether this version proxies or filters image URLs in posts. Mail scanners that pre-fetch links do the same, see the idempotency finding. Existing code changes the level through `POST /t/:id/notifications` (the `set_notifications` action, which is in the ensure_logged_in list at line 18). The page could render a confirmation and send that request.

JSON request with mismatched slug is redirected to the HTML URL

`workingHours.find(...)` returns true as soon as ANY block that includes the day has the slot outside its range, and that `true` makes the function return `false`. Shifted override times wrap past midnight and are silently dropped or placed on the wrong day

The `hour()` call wraps modulo 24h, with no clamping like `getWorkingHours` does (packages/lib/availability.ts:87-111). If `offset` (invitee offset minus organizer offset) pushes the override over midnight, the start is on one day and the end is on the next. For example, a 09:00–17:00 override with an 18h offset gives start 03:00 and end 11:00, and with a 10h offset gives start 19:00 and end 03:00. In the second case `end < start`, so `buildSlots` skips it (`if (start >= end) continue`, line 68). The user's regular working hours were already removed at lines 228-243, so that day shows no slots and nothing reports an error.

The override is also selected as `activeOverrides` (line 206) by its unshifted instant against the invitee's day, while the minutes are computed after shifting, so the two disagree for large offsets. The shifted time should be clamped or split across days, as `getWorkingHours` does.

Dead comparison and UTC-day matching in the date-override check

Line 114 compares two `Dayjs` objects with `===`. That is reference equality and is always false, so the branch never runs. If a zero-length override was meant to block the day, use `.isSame()` or compare `valueOf()`.

The override is matched to a slot by the UTC calendar day of the shifted override start (110-111). For an organizer far from UTC (e.g. UTC+10, 09:00–17:00 local = 23:00–07:00 UTC) the override range spans two UTC days. Slots on the later UTC day do not match, so `dateOverrideExist` stays false for them and they are judged by the normal working-hours block instead of the override. Compare against the override's [start,end) instant range rather than a calendar-day string.

Redundant parsing and repeated computation in override mapping

`dayjs(override.start.toString())` goes through `Date.toString()`, which drops milliseconds and relies on string parsing. Use `dayjs(override.start)` or `dayjs.utc(override.start)`. `dayjs(override.start).utc().add(offset,'minute')` is also computed four times; compute each shifted value once. `timeZone` is optional in `TimeRange` (packages/types/schedule.d.ts:5), and `.tz(undefined)` here falls back to the server's local zone. That is harmless today because `getSchedule` always sets it, but it would silently use the wrong zone for any other caller.

The added case checks a single invitee zone (+6:00) against an organizer in +5:30. It does not cover an invitee whose offset puts the override across midnight (see lib/slots.ts finding), a host with two blocks on one day, or a slot that runs past the end of a working block. The last two are the paths where the new `checkIfIsAvailable` working-hours logic is wrong. Round-robin and fixed-host date-override scenarios named in the PR description are also untested.

Failing update in catch block aborts the whole cron run

The `prisma.workflowReminder.update` added in the `catch` (lines 190-197) is not wrapped in its own try/catch. If it rejects (DB error, or the row was deleted concurrently, which gives P2025 on a missing record), the exception escapes the `for` loop and the handler. Every later reminder in the batch is skipped and the cron returns a 500. Before this change the catch only logged, so one bad reminder could not stop the batch. Wrap the update in a try/catch, or log first and guard the update.

Delete branch for retryCount > 1 is not limited to SMS reminders

The second `OR` branch (lines 38-42) has no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` condition, so this SMS cron deletes any `WorkflowReminder` with `retryCount > 1`, whatever its method. A grep of packages/ finds `retryCount` on WorkflowReminder only in this file and the schema, so nothing else increments it today. The deletion still covers email and WhatsApp rows if another job ever starts using the column. Scope it: `{ method: WorkflowMethods.SMS, retryCount: { gt: 1 } }`.

Read-modify-write retry counter

`retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1` (lines 184 and 195) uses the value read at the start of the run. Overlapping cron invocations, or a run slower than the cron interval, can both write the same value, so a failing reminder gets more retries than intended. `retryCount: { increment: 1 }` is atomic and avoids this. The same duplicated update appears in both the `else` branch and the `catch`, so it could be a small helper.

Reminders for locked users are silently deleted after two runs

`twilio.scheduleSMS` returns `undefined` when SMS sending is locked for the user or team (twilioProvider.ts:90-95). The new `else` branch counts that as a failure, and the reminder is deleted once `retryCount` exceeds 1. An unlock shortly afterwards would no longer send reminders that were previously kept until `scheduledDate`. Confirm this is intended. Also, the threshold `gt: 1` allows only two attempts, which is a very low retry budget for transient errors such as Twilio or rate-limit failures.

Public auth/filter conditions are returned without outer parentheses

`getAuthorizationConditions()` and `getFilterConditions()` are public, and the org/team auth fragment is `(A) OR (B)` and the event-type filter is `(x) OR (y)`, both with no outer parentheses. `getBaseConditions` wraps each one, so it is correct. A caller that interpolates the fragment directly, for example ``WHERE ${auth} AND "createdAt" > ...``, gets `(A) OR (B) AND ...` because AND binds tighter than OR. That would let bookings outside the authorised scope through, since the auth fragment is the access-control boundary. Consider wrapping the final result of `buildOrgAuthorizationCondition`, `buildTeamAuthorizationCondition` and the event-type filter in `( ... )`, or making only `getBaseConditions` public. The same applies to lines 119-122, 204-207 and 106. The tests assert the unwrapped shape, so they would need updating too. I found no other callers in the repository, so this is a robustness point rather than a bug today.

Loose public options type removes compile-time check for the team scope

`InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions` makes `teamId` optional for every scope, so `scope: "team"` without `teamId` now compiles. Zod then rejects it at runtime and the service silently returns `1=0`, an empty result with no error. The old constructor took the discriminated union type, which caught this at compile time. A discriminated union type (or `z.input` of the schema) would keep the check. If the loose type is deliberate, for example to accept tRPC input, a comment saying so would help.

Dead branches in getBaseConditions

`getAuthorizationConditions()` always returns a `Prisma.Sql`, which is always truthy. So the `else if (filterConditions)` and `else` branches that return `filterConditions` or `NOTHING_CONDITION` can never run. Simplify to `return filterConditions ? Prisma.sql`(${auth}) AND (${filterConditions})` : auth`.

Lost coverage: caching tests removed, and the new SQL paths are barely run against the database

The Caching tests were deleted. The `cachedAuthConditions` and `cachedFilterConditions` logic still exists in the service, so it is now untested. Only the user scope is executed against the DB, in the `getBaseConditions` test. The org and team fragments with `ANY(array)` and the `isTeamBooking` OR-combination are checked only by `toEqual` on the `Sql` object. That does not show the SQL is valid or returns the right rows, for example when the array parameter is bound as `int[]`. There is also no test for `getBaseConditions` when the user is not an owner or admin (`1=0`), or for the team scope with no members (the new omitted-branch case).

Google credential is saved as the safeParse result object, not the token

`parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the zod `safeParse` result (`{ success, data }`, see parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:29). Line 97 assigns that to `key`, and line 100 writes it to `credential.key`. After the first token refresh the stored key is `{ success: true, data: {...} }`. The old code stored the parsed data. The next `GoogleCalendarService` constructor then calls `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` (line 75) and throws, so every Google Calendar credential breaks after its first refresh. Use `parsed.data` and check `parsed.success`, as the Zoom and Salesforce call sites do.

`prisma` is used but never imported

Line 96 calls `prisma.credential.update`. The file has no `prisma` import (the only match for `prisma` in the file is this line). It fails type-check, and at runtime it throws a ReferenceError inside `getClient`. That rejects `this.conn`, so every Salesforce calendar operation fails. Add `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma";`.

Salesforce now refreshes on every instantiation, then builds the connection with the old access token

`getClient` runs in the constructor (line 57). The new code POSTs to Salesforce's token endpoint on every instantiation, whether or not the token is expired. It stores the new token (line 96), but the `jsforce.Connection` at lines 101-108 still uses `credentialKey.access_token` from before the refresh. So the refresh buys nothing for the current request, and it adds a network call and a possible rate-limit hit per instantiation. `response.statusText !== "OK"` (line 86) also throws for any response with an empty status text (e.g. HTTP/2). Salesforce is also the only provider that bypasses `refreshOAuthTokens`, so credential sync does not apply to it, yet it still calls `parseRefreshTokenResponse`. Refresh only when expired, use the new `access_token` for the connection, and route the call through `refreshOAuthTokens`. Also confirm that adding a refresh to Salesforce is intended in this PR.

`minimumTokenResponseSchema` uses computed keys that evaluate to "[object Object]"

`[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` are both the string `"[object Object]"`, because zod types do not override `toString`. The schema is therefore `{ access_token: string, "[object Object]": unknown | optional }`. The second key overwrites the first, so there is no number requirement and no expiry check. `z.object` also strips unknown keys by default, so `expires_in`, `expiry_date`, `scope` and the like never reach `data`. In credential-sync mode the consumers read fields that are gone: Zoom computes `Date.now() + newTokens.expires_in * 1000`, which is NaN (zoomvideo VideoApiAdapter.ts:122), and Office365 loses `expires_in`. The result is an unusable stored key or a refresh on every call. Use `z.object({ access_token: z.string() }).passthrough()` plus an explicit expiry check, for example `.refine` over any numeric field, or require a named field.

Placeholder refresh_token overwrites the real one, in non-sync mode too

When the response has no `refresh_token`, the helper sets the literal string `"refresh_token"`. This runs outside credential-sync mode as well. Office365 calendar's schema has `refresh_token` optional (office365calendar CalendarService.ts:56), and its caller spreads the parsed data over the stored credentials (line 264). A refresh response without a new refresh token therefore replaces the stored valid refresh token with the literal `"refresh_token"`, and the credential cannot refresh again. Previously the old value survived the spread. Apply the placeholder only in sync mode, or have callers keep the existing refresh token.

In sync mode a raw fetch Response is returned to callers that expect an axios/SDK/googleapis shape

The sync branch returns the `fetch` `Response`, but several callers read a different shape from it:
- Google reads `res?.data` (googlecalendar CalendarService.ts:94). `Response` has no `data`, so it throws a TypeError, which is swallowed (the catch returns the old auth, line 108).
- Zoho CRM and Zoho Bigin read `.data.error` and `.data.access_token` (zohocrm CalendarService.ts:217; zoho-bigin CalendarService.ts:96).
- HubSpot reads `.expiresIn` and `.accessToken` directly on the result (hubspot CalendarService.ts:192).

None of them calls `.json()`. Only callers that run `handle*Response` or `handleErrorsJson` on the response work in sync mode. Normalise the sync response inside the helper, or have each caller adapt it.

Sync endpoint request is unauthenticated, has no timeout, and the status is unchecked

The POST to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` carries only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug`, with no shared secret or header. It has no timeout, and a non-2xx response is not checked here. Any party that can reach the endpoint can request tokens for an arbitrary userId. An error body is also passed on as if it were a token response. Consider sending the webhook secret (or a signed header), setting a timeout, and failing on `!response.ok`.

Credential id is passed where `refreshOAuthTokens` expects the user id

The third argument of `refreshOAuthTokens` is `userId` (refreshOAuthTokens.ts:3). Here `credentialId` (`credential.id`, line 53) is passed. In sync mode this asks the sync endpoint for the wrong user's tokens, because a credential id is not a user id. It also skips the intended `userId` null check. Pass `credential.userId`; `biginAuth` has the credential in scope and must pass it down to `refreshAccessToken`.

Dead `success` check and removed error logging change behaviour on invalid MS responses

`parseRefreshTokenResponse` throws when parsing fails and otherwise always returns `success: true`. So `tokenResponse.success && tokenResponse.data` is always `data`. The removed `console.error` branch (which logged the zod error and the MS response) is gone, so a malformed MS response now throws a generic "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned" error without the response body. Previously it was logged and the old credentials were kept. Simplify the spread and keep the diagnostic log.

Body validation and decryption errors become unhandled 500s; secret compared non-constant-time; no method check

`appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` (line 31), `symmetricDecrypt` and `JSON.parse` (lines 57-59) all throw on bad input. Nothing catches them, so a malformed request, wrong key or bad ciphertext gives a 500 instead of a 400. Use `safeParse` and a try/catch that returns 400. The secret check (lines 24-27) uses `!==` on a string, which is not timing-safe, so use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on equal-length buffers. The handler also accepts any HTTP method, so restrict it to POST. The decrypted `keys` are written to `credential.key` (lines 78, 85) without any per-app shape validation. A bad payload would silently corrupt a user's credential.

Unrelated hard-coded slug in redirectUri

`appConfig.slug` was replaced by the literal `zoho-bigin` in `redirectUri`, while `appConfig` is still imported and used for `getAppKeysFromSlug(appConfig.slug)` (line 12) and the scope (line 22). The change has nothing to do with credential sync and adds a second source of truth for the slug. Revert it.

No tests for the new webhook or the refresh helpers

The PR adds a credential-write webhook, a token-response parser and a refresh wrapper used by about ten integrations. It adds no tests. A unit test of `parseRefreshTokenResponse` would have caught the bugs in this file and the Google misuse (Google CalendarService.ts:97).

Reminder cancellation is now fire-and-forget, so the `cancelled` flag can be lost without any error

Before this PR the reminder rows were deleted through Prisma promises that the callers awaited (`await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` in handleCancelBooking, `await Promise.all(remindersToDelete)` in bookings.tsx and workflows.tsx). Now the DB write (`prisma.workflowReminder.update({cancelled:true})` here, `delete` in smsReminderManager.ts:182) happens inside `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` / `deleteScheduledSMSReminder`. Every caller invokes them without `await` (handleCancelBooking.ts:487-491, bookings.tsx:489-493, workflows.tsx:213-217, 377-381, 520-524, 575-579, handleNewBooking.ts:966-972). The handlers return right after, so on a serverless runtime the invocation can be frozen before the write runs. The email is then never marked cancelled and is sent for a cancelled or rescheduled booking, with no error anywhere. Await the calls (for example collect the promises and `await Promise.all(...)`) in each caller.

The `try/catch` in handleNewBooking.ts:964-975 also cannot catch anything, because the promises are not awaited and the helpers already swallow their own errors.

One failing SendGrid cancel aborts all remaining cancellations, and no row is deleted until the whole loop succeeds

The loop awaits `client.request` for each reminder inside one `try`. The Prisma `delete` calls are only queued (they are lazy) and only run at `await Promise.all(workflowRemindersToDelete)` after the loop. If any request rejects (batch already cancelled or too close to its send time, invalid id, rate limit), the catch at line 75 swallows it. The remaining reminders are not cancelled, and the ones already cancelled at SendGrid are not deleted either. Every 15-minute run (see .github/workflows/cron-scheduleEmailReminders.yml:8) re-selects the same rows and hits the same failing reminder first, so later reminders are never cancelled and their emails go out for cancelled bookings. Put the try/catch inside the loop and delete each row right after its successful cancel.

Why do only some callers cancel immediately, and why was the SendGrid DELETE dropped?

`immediateDelete=true` cancels at SendGrid but leaves the DB row (it only disappears when the cron's `deleteMany` runs after `scheduledDate`). The default path only marks `cancelled` and relies on the 15-minute cron, which only looks at reminders whose `scheduledDate` is within the next hour. So a cancel, reschedule, step edit or event-type removal leaves the email live in SendGrid for up to an hour. If the cancel happens less than about 15 minutes before send, it can go out. Is that window intended? Also, the old code followed the cancel with `DELETE /v3/user/scheduled_sends/{id}` and that call is now gone in both paths. Is leaving cancelled batch ids in SendGrid intended?

Unused `Prisma` import and whitespace-only churn inside a comment block

`Prisma` is now imported as a value but nothing else in the file uses it. Its only use, `Prisma.BatchPayload`, was removed in this PR. There is also no trailing comma after it. Lines 904-962 only lose their indentation. That region sits inside a `/* ... */` comment, so this is formatter noise that hides the real changes in the diff. Revert it.

No tests for the new cancel-via-cron flow

No test covers any of it, for example marking a reminder cancelled, the cron cancelling and deleting it, or a SendGrid failure in the loop.

Team admin check uses && with isTeamOwner, so only owners pass

`isTeamAdmin` already returns the membership for role ADMIN or OWNER (`packages/lib/server/queries/teams/index.ts:264-284`), and `isTeamOwner` is true only for OWNER (`:286-295`). Blacklist check is case-sensitive on the guest side, and base-email handling is skipped

The blacklist entries are lowercased on line 71, but `guest` is compared as submitted. If `BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS` contains `spam@x.com`, then `Spam@X.com` passes. `handleNewBooking.ts:736-743` lowercases both sides and uses `extractBaseEmail`, so `+alias` variants are caught there. This path skips that, which lets someone get a blocked address onto a booking and trigger an email to it. Lowercase the guest and reuse `extractBaseEmail`, as `handleNewBooking.ts:742` does.

Server does not dedupe the submitted guests or compare existing attendees case-insensitively

The unique-email rule is enforced only in the dialog (`AddGuestsDialog.tsx:26-29`). `addGuests.schema.ts:5` accepts any array. A direct tRPC call with `[a@x.com, a@x.com]` passes the filter on lines 74-78, because it only compares against existing attendees. `createMany` then inserts two attendee rows for the same address. `A@x.com` also passes against an existing `a@x.com`. Consider adding `.min(1)` and a `.max()` to the schema, since each guest triggers an outbound email.

Attendees are committed before the fallible steps, with no recovery path

`prisma.booking.update` (lines 92-106) persists the new attendees. After that come `getTranslation`, `getUsersCredentials`, `new EventManager` and `updateCalendarAttendees` (lines 108-165), none of them in a try/catch. If one throws, the client gets a 500 and an error toast, but the guests are already stored and no emails go out. Retrying then hits `uniqueGuests.length === 0` (line 80) and shows 'Emails must be unique and valid', so the user has no way to get the guests notified. Move the DB write after the calendar update, or handle the failure explicitly. Also check what `updateCalendarAttendees` returns: its result is ignored, and it returns early without error when `booking.references` is empty (`EventManager.ts:597-600`).

sendAddGuestsEmails ignores the event type's host/attendee email-disable settings

New-guest detection uses the raw request list, and team-member branch is dead for this caller

The handler passes `guests` (the raw input, line 168 of `addGuests.handler.ts`), not `uniqueGuests`. Invalid-email banner is never cleared on success or when the dialog is dismissed otherwise

onError message is always truthy, so the fallback key is dead and the toast is noisy

`${err.data?.code}: ${t(err.message)}` is always a non-empty string, so `message || t("unable_to_add_guests")` never falls back, and the `unable_to_add_guests` string added to `common.json` is never used. Show `t(err.message)` only for the known keys the handler throws, and otherwise `t("unable_to_add_guests")`. Separately, with zero rows, `handleAdd` returns silently (line 49-51): after removing every row, clicking Add does nothing.

Schema is rebuilt on every render and duplicates the server schema

`ZAddGuestsInputSchema` is created inside the component body each render, and it shadows the name of the server schema in `addGuests.schema.ts`. Move it to module scope. Use `.toLowerCase()` for the duplicate comparison so it matches what the server should do.

Copy of the form-builder MultiEmail; imports the package barrel from inside the package; hardcoded tooltip

No check of booking status, end time, or seat configuration before adding attendees

No tests for a new permission-gated mutation

The authorization branches (organizer, attendee, team admin or owner), the blacklist and dedupe filtering, and the email recipient split (new guest versus existing attendee) are all untested. The `&&` bug on line 48 is the kind of defect a permission test would catch.

A backup code alone logs in, because a dummy totpCode skips the password check

The password is only verified when `!credentials.totpCode` (line 121). The new branch at line 131 runs when `credentials.backupCode` is set. Backup code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write

The code list is read in `findUnique` at line 73, then rewritten whole at lines 149-156. Two concurrent logins with the same code can both pass `indexOf` before either update lands, so a "single use" code is accepted twice. The same applies to disable.ts, though that endpoint deletes all codes afterwards.

Closing the dialog on the backup-codes step by Escape or an outside click leaves the UI wrong and the codes lost

"Please generate them in your settings" points to a feature that does not exist

The only place codes are generated is `setup.ts`, during the enable flow, and nothing lets a user regenerate them. A non-string backupCode in the request body causes an unhandled 500

`req.body.backupCode.replaceAll(...)` throws a TypeError if the JSON body has a number or object. Component is named TwoFactor

Hangout-link patch uses `selectedCalendar` that can now be undefined

isAccessTokenId never checks the grant shortcut (inverted condition and wrong offset)

The token id is `<2 session><2 tokenType><2 grant>:<uuid>`, so the grant shortcut is `substring(4, 6)`. The code takes `substring(3, 5)`, which is the last char of the token type plus the first char of the grant. It also returns `false` when that substring *equals* the expected shortcut. Because the offsets are wrong, the equality can never hold for a valid id, so the check never rejects anything. The matcher then accepts any `x:uuid` string with one colon. A regression where `expectCodeToToken` or `expectRefresh` produced the wrong grant, or `na`, would pass. If only the offset were fixed, every correct id would fail because of the inverted condition. Use `!items[0].substring(4, 6).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)` and check `items[0].length() == 6` first. `describeTo` should also say what is expected, for example "access token id with grant shortcut X and UUID".
